statement: In the multiplication AB × AB = CAB, AB is a two-digit number and CAB is a three-digit number. Different letters stand for different digits. What is the two-digit number AB?

choices.misconception: I guessed the number must end in 5 and took the smallest such number, 15, without checking that 15 × 15 = 225 does not end in 15.
I matched only the last digit: 16 × 16 = 256 ends in 6, but I did not check that the square ends in 16.
I found that 76 × 76 ends in 76 but missed that its square, 5776, has four digits, not three.
I gave the square CAB instead of the number AB.

hints: The square of AB must end in the two digits AB themselves.
The square has only three digits, which limits how big AB can be. The last digit of B × B must be B, which leaves very few choices for B. Combine both limits and test what remains.
AB is at most 31, since 32 × 32 = 1024. The digit B must be 0, 1, 5 or 6, so test 10, 11, 15, 16, 20, 21, 25, 26, 30 and 31.

solutions.reliable: Since CAB has three digits, AB is at most 31 (32 × 32 = 1024). The last digit of B × B must be B, so B is 0, 1, 5 or 6. The candidates and their squares are 10: 100, 11: 121, 15: 225, 16: 256, 20: 400, 21: 441, 25: 625, 26: 676, 30: 900, 31: 961. Only 625 ends in the original number, and it gives A = 2, B = 5, C = 6, all different. So AB = 25. The transferable idea: a last-digit filter and a size bound together shrink a digit puzzle to a short list.
solutions.elegant: AB × AB ends in AB exactly when AB × (AB - 1) is a multiple of 100. Two consecutive numbers share no factor, so one of them is a multiple of 25 and the other a multiple of 4. The only options are 25 (with 24) and 76 (with 75), and 76 squared has four digits.

whyOnTest: Cryptarithm questions reward combining a last-digit filter with a size bound; the trap answers 16 and 76 each pass only one of the two checks.
